subject: stats
title: Presentation of Statistical Data
objectives: Classify data geographically, personally, qualitatively and quantitatively.
Construct a grouped frequency distribution, including class limits, boundaries, marks and cumulative frequencies.
Present data in tabular form and choose the appropriate diagram for a given dataset.
Construct and interpret histograms, frequency polygons, bar charts, pie charts and ogives.
study:
Raw data is a mass of unorganised figures that offers little insight until it is classified, tabulated and presented. Data can be classified on four bases: Geographical (Spatial) classification, organised by country, region, state or city; Personal classification, based on personal attributes such as age, gender or occupation; Qualitative (Descriptive) classification, based on non-numerical attributes such as department or blood group — these have no inherent order (nominal data), though some carry a logical order (ordinal data, e.g. job grades Junior/Middle/Senior); and Quantitative (Numerical) classification, based on numerical values, using class intervals for continuous data.

Key termFrequency distribution — a tabular arrangement of data into classes with the corresponding number of observations (frequency) in each class.

To construct a grouped frequency distribution: find the Range (Maximum − Minimum), decide the number of classes (usually 5–20, guided by Sturges' Rule: k = 1 + 3.322 × log₁₀(n)), calculate Class Width (Range ÷ Number of Classes), set mutually exclusive and exhaustive class boundaries, then tally frequencies. Key vocabulary: the Class Limits are the stated lower/upper values of a class (e.g. 20–29); the Class Boundaries are the true continuous limits, found by extending each limit by half a unit (e.g. 19.5–29.5); the Class Mark is the midpoint, the average of the lower and upper limits (e.g. 34.5 for 30–39); Frequency is the count in a class; Relative Frequency is frequency ÷ n; and Cumulative Frequency is the running total up to a given class. Where class widths are unequal, plot Frequency Density (frequency ÷ class width) instead of raw frequency.

Exam tipClass limits and class boundaries are commonly confused. Boundaries (not limits) go on the horizontal axis of a histogram, and boundaries are what's used to compute the median from grouped data.

Data can be presented in tables — simple (one characteristic) or complex/two-way (cross-classifying two characteristics, e.g. staff by department and gender) — or graphically. Eight diagram types matter most: the Histogram (adjacent bars over class boundaries, for continuous grouped data), the Frequency Polygon (frequencies plotted against class marks and joined with straight lines, closed at both ends), the Ogive (cumulative frequency plotted against upper class boundaries, forming an S-shaped curve — a 'less than' ogive rises left to right, a 'more than' ogive falls left to right), the Bar Chart (simple, for comparing discrete categories), the Multiple Bar Chart (grouped bars comparing two or more datasets side by side), the Component Bar Chart (stacked bars showing sub-category composition), the Pie Chart (a circle divided into sectors, each sector's angle calculated as (frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360°), and the Line Graph (points joined by lines, for trends over time).

The ogive specifically is used to estimate the median, quartiles, deciles and percentiles graphically, and to find how many observations fall above or below a given value.
recap:
• 4 classification types: Geographical, Personal, Qualitative (nominal/ordinal), Quantitative.
  • Frequency distribution construction: Range → number of classes (Sturges' Rule) → class width → boundaries → tally.
  • Class limits (stated) vs class boundaries (true limits, ±0.5); class mark = midpoint; frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
  • Tables: simple (one characteristic) vs complex/two-way (cross-classified).
  • 8 diagram types: Histogram, Frequency Polygon, Ogive, Bar Chart, Multiple Bar Chart, Component Bar Chart, Pie Chart, Line Graph.
  • Pie chart angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.
  • Ogive estimates median, quartiles, deciles, percentiles; 'less than' rises, 'more than' falls.

quiz.q: Data organised by country, region, state or city is called …… classification.
quiz.why: Geographical (spatial) classification organises data by physical location.

quiz.q: Data classified based on personal attributes such as age, gender or occupation is called …… classification.
quiz.why: Personal classification groups data by attributes of the individuals themselves.

quiz.q: Data classified by non-numerical attributes such as department or blood group, with no inherent order, is called …… classification.
quiz.why: Qualitative (descriptive) classification groups data by non-numerical, nominal attributes.

quiz.q: Job grades such as Junior, Middle and Senior, which carry a logical order, are an example of …… data.
quiz.why: Ordinal data has categories with a meaningful order, unlike nominal data which does not.

quiz.q: A frequency distribution is best described as:
opts: A method of collecting primary data
A random arrangement of raw data
A specialised type of pie chart
A table of classes paired with their frequencies
quiz.why: A frequency distribution organises raw data into classes, each paired with its count (frequency).

quiz.q: Sturges' Rule, used to decide the number of classes in a frequency distribution, is calculated as:
quiz.why: Sturges' Rule uses the sample size n and a log base 10 calculation to suggest an appropriate number of classes.

quiz.q: Class width in a frequency distribution is calculated as:
opts: The number of classes in the distribution
Upper class limit plus lower class limit
quiz.why: Class width is the span of a class, found by subtracting the lower boundary from the upper boundary.

quiz.q: The class boundaries of the class interval 20–29 are:
quiz.why: Class boundaries extend the stated limits by half a unit on each side, turning 20-29 into 19.5-29.5.

quiz.q: The class mark (mid-point) of the class interval 30–39 is:
quiz.why: The class mark is the average of the lower and upper limits: (30+39)/2 = 34.5.

quiz.q: The running total of frequencies up to and including a given class is called:
quiz.why: Cumulative frequency is specifically the running total, not the count within a single class.

quiz.q: Frequency divided by class width, used when class widths are unequal, is called frequency ……
quiz.why: Frequency density adjusts for unequal class widths, and is plotted on histograms in place of raw frequency in that case.

quiz.q: Which diagram type is most appropriate for continuous, grouped data with adjoining bars and no gaps?
quiz.why: A histogram's bars touch because the underlying data is continuous, unlike an ordinary bar chart for discrete categories.

quiz.q: A frequency polygon is constructed by plotting frequency against:
quiz.why: A frequency polygon joins points plotted at each class's midpoint (class mark), not its limits or boundaries.

quiz.q: The angle of a sector in a pie chart is calculated as:
quiz.why: A pie chart's sectors are proportions of a full circle (360°), not a percentage (which would use ×100).

quiz.q: A cumulative frequency curve, plotted against upper class boundaries, is called a(n):
quiz.why: The ogive is specifically the cumulative frequency curve, distinct from the histogram or frequency polygon.

quiz.q: Which chart type shows the composition of totals using stacked bars subdivided into sub-categories?
quiz.why: A component (stacked) bar chart divides each bar to show how sub-categories make up the total.

quiz.q: Which chart type compares two or more datasets side by side using grouped bars per category?
quiz.why: A multiple bar chart groups separate bars for each dataset next to one another within each category.

quiz.q: All the following are estimated from an ogive, EXCEPT:
quiz.why: The ogive estimates positional measures like the median, quartiles and deciles; class width is a fixed input decided before the distribution is built, not read off the ogive.

quiz.q: A 'less than' ogive, as distinguished from a 'more than' ogive, is one that:
quiz.why: A 'less than' ogive accumulates frequency as values increase, so it rises; a 'more than' ogive falls as values increase.

quiz.q: Tables that show the cross-classification of two characteristics, such as staff by department and gender, are called …… tables.
quiz.why: A simple table shows one characteristic; a complex or two-way table cross-classifies two or more.

cards.back: A tabular arrangement of data into classes with the corresponding frequency in each class.
Limits are the stated values (e.g. 20-29); boundaries are the true continuous limits, found by extending limits by half a unit (19.5-29.5).
The midpoint of a class: average of the lower and upper limits.
k = 1 + 3.322 x log10(n) — used to decide the number of classes in a frequency distribution.
Frequency divided by class width; used on histograms when class widths are unequal.
Adjacent bars over class boundaries, for continuous grouped data — bars touch, unlike a bar chart.
Frequencies plotted against class marks (midpoints) and joined with straight lines.
Cumulative frequency plotted against upper class boundaries; S-shaped; estimates median, quartiles, deciles.
Bars subdivided to show how sub-categories make up each total.
